title: The passive of the present system

objectives.can: Recognise passive forms of the present, imperfect and future and parse them.

explanation.summary: In the active voice the subject acts; in the passive the subject receives the action. For the present, imperfect and future tenses Latin makes the passive by changing the personal endings of the active, and the Vulgate is full of such verbs: things are called, given, sent, judged and raised.

sections.heading: Active and passive
body: Compare *exaltat*, 'he raises up', with *exaltabitur*, 'he will be raised up'. In the first the subject does the raising; in the second the subject has it done to him. Voice is the name for this property of a verb, and the corpus records it as Voice=Act or Voice=Pass.
Only a verb that can take an object has a true passive. What was the object in the active sentence becomes the subject in the passive one: 'God raises him' becomes 'he is raised by God'.

sections.heading: The passive endings
body: The tense signs do not change. The present, the imperfect (-ba-) and the future (-bi-, -b-, or -e-) are built exactly as in the active. Only the personal endings are replaced, and the replacement is regular: -o or -m becomes -r, and in the third person singular and plural a -t or -nt becomes -tur or -ntur.

The table sets the two voices side by side. The endings of the second person plural (-mini) and the second person singular (-ris) are the ones to learn by heart; the others are easy to guess from the active.

sections.heading: Three tenses, one pattern
body: Present: *vocat* (he calls) becomes *vocatur* (he is called); *vocant* becomes *vocantur*. Imperfect: *vocabatur* (he was being called, or used to be called), *vocabantur* for the plural. Future: *vocabitur* (he will be called), *vocabuntur* for the plural.

In the first and second conjugations the future has -bi- (-bor, -beris, -bitur). In the third and fourth it has -e- (-etur, -entur). A third-conjugation verb therefore differs by one vowel between present and future: -itur is present, -etur is future. Read that vowel with care.

sections.heading: Who does it, and with what
body: The person who performs a passive action is the agent, and Latin puts the agent in the ablative with *a* or *ab* ('by'): in *convincitur ab omnibus* the whole company is the agent. Something that is only an instrument, not a person acting, stands in the bare ablative, the ablative of means: in *igni comburuntur* the weeds are burnt 'with fire' and no preposition is used.
Many passive sentences name no agent at all. The reader supplies it from context, and in Scripture it is very often God.

sections.heading: In the library
body: Almost every passive form in the texts is third person. Forms in the first and second person exist (*vocaberis* is in John 1) but are rare, so the paradigms below are in the third person, singular and plural, and show the three tenses side by side.

misunderstandings: A passive verb is not 'is doing': *vocatur* means 'is called' or 'is being called', never 'is calling'. In English the passive needs a form of 'to be'; in Latin the ending alone does the work.
Not every verb with a passive ending is passive. Deponent verbs such as *loquor* look passive but are active in meaning; they have their own lesson. The corpus tags them as active.
-tur is not the sign of the present tense. It marks the passive voice in all three tenses: *vocatur*, *vocabatur*, *vocabitur* are present, imperfect and future. The tense is shown before the ending.

deeper.heading: A second singular in -re
body: Grammars note that the second person singular passive also had a shorter ending in -re beside -ris, and the form is found in poetry and in some later writers. The forms in the library are overwhelmingly in -ris, which is the one to learn.

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: Because every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: Two active verbs and two passives, set against each other. *exaltat* and *humiliat* are active: 'he exalts', 'he humbles'. *humiliabitur* and *exaltabitur* are future passive, third person singular: 'he will be humbled', 'he will be exalted'. The tense sign -bi- is the same as in an active future; only the ending -tur has changed. No agent is named.

examples.analysis: *convincitur* and *dijudicatur* are present passive, third person singular. Each has an agent introduced by *ab*, 'by'. This is the pattern for a person who acts: *ab* with the ablative.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: Even as cockle therefore is gathered up, and burnt with fire: so shall it be at the end of the world.

examples.analysis: *colliguntur* and *comburuntur* are present passive, third person plural, agreeing with the plural subject. The word *igni* ('with fire') stands in the ablative without a preposition: the means of burning. The analyser is unsure whether it reads *igni* as ablative or dative here, which is why it is not highlighted.

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.english: And there came also together to Jerusalem a multitude out of the neighboring cities, bringing sick persons, and such as were troubled with unclean spirits; who were all healed.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *curabantur* is imperfect passive, third person plural: 'they were being healed', with the -ba- of the imperfect and the ending -ntur. The imperfect describes a continuing or repeated action; here the healing went on among the many who were brought.

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: And I say to you, Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *dabitur* and *aperietur* are both future passive, third person singular. *dabitur* is first conjugation in form (-bi-), while *aperietur* is a fourth-conjugation verb with the -e- future. No agent is stated; the reader understands that God gives and opens.

reading.why: Asking, seeking and knocking, answered by passive verbs in the future: it will be given, it will be opened. A short passage in which the passive hides the giver, and the next verses name him.
